scope: Selected Old Babylonian Nippur evidence; qualifications in main report

claims.title: Hire mediated through a father
claims.claim: BE 6/2 51 records Idin-Ištar, explicitly the son of Nabi-Šamaš, hired from Nabi-Šamaš by Lu-Ninsianna for a fixed term with a monthly grain payment.
claims.context: Nippur legal document; Istanbul Ni 1847; no room-level context established
claims.primary: BE 6/2 51, Ni 1847; P1909 p. 43; catalogue p. 151. Monthly amount: 80 qa of grain in the edition.
claims.secondary: Poebel’s suggestion of payment at the end of the term is commentary, not an explicit clause.
claims.counter: The occupation, age, residence, precise payment recipient, and ownership status are not stated.
claims.rationale: The hiring parties, kin relation, term, and rate are explicit in the published text; confidence is confined to those particulars.
claims.limit: One hire agreement; not a standard wage, a census of hired workers, or proof of child labor or free self-contracting.
claims.relevance: A kin relationship and a paid work arrangement appear together without becoming the same relationship.
claims.interpretations: The father mediates the agreement. Whether he exercised ownership, guardianship, household authority, or another legal capacity cannot be decided from these clauses alone.

claims.title: Kinship and maintenance obligations
claims.claim: Nippur agreements connect filial or adoptive relationships with inheritance-linked maintenance obligations; these are not identical to ownership of the obligated person.
claims.context: BE 6/2 28: Ibkuša and two sons; BE 6/2 48: Awilia, Naramtum, and three sons; Nippur
claims.secondary: P1909 discusses maintenance and adoption together. The report retains the clauses without adopting a universal old-age explanation.
claims.counter: Maintenance supplies do not identify who produced them. Birth/adoptive relations do not establish age or co-residence.
claims.rationale: Two independently identified documents explicitly tie support and property expectations to filial relationships.
claims.limit: The specified agreements, not all adopted persons, all sons, or all household labor.
claims.relevance: Distinguishes support obligations and created kinship from enslavement and occupational work.
claims.interpretations: BE 28 places the son by the wife and the adopted son under parallel support duties. BE 48 gives Naramtum a filial relationship with Awilia’s sons and provides maintenance with property-related sanctions.

claims.title: Enslaved people in estate allocation
claims.claim: BE 6/2 23 allocates four named enslaved people between the shares of Narubtum and Ur-Pabilsaĝa.
claims.context: Nippur; Ur-Pabilsaĝa/interconnected family dossier; Istanbul Ni 1917
claims.etype: Primary edition, with modern disagreement check
claims.primary: BE 6/2 23, P1909 pp. 20–22; catalogue p. 147. Ali-aḫuša and Iškur-rīm-ilī in Narubtum’s portion; Dumqi-Ištar and Taribum in Ur-Pabilsaĝa’s.
claims.secondary: VW2018 pp. 21–22 records competing reconstructions of the closing kinship/adoption clause.
claims.counter: The contested genealogy does not erase the allocations. The text does not assign these people particular jobs or identify their own family ties.
claims.rationale: The named people and their allocation are explicit; the narrow claim does not require choosing the disputed genealogy.
claims.limit: A property division, not a headcount of co-residents or an occupational roster; no transfer itinerary established.
claims.relevance: Shows ownership interests passing through family property arrangements while residence and labor remain unrecorded.
claims.interpretations: Enslavement is supported by the legal allocation context, not by treating the gender designations alone as universally equivalent to “slave.”

claims.title: Conditional enslavement is not an accomplished sale
claims.claim: BE 6/2 24 stipulates sale following adoptees’ repudiation of their adoptive parents; the clause does not report that repudiation or sale occurred.
claims.context: Nippur; Ea-idinnam, Kuritum, Ili-idinnam, and Ili-ummati; CBS 10891, P266084
claims.primary: BE 6/2 24, P1909 pp. 27–29; catalogue p. 148. Additional conditional language is present in BE 6/2 57.
claims.secondary: P1909’s translation distinguishes the adoption from future breach conditions.
claims.counter: No enforcement event is documented in this text; it does not establish prior enslaved status.
claims.rationale: The conditional syntax and the completed adoption are different parts of the agreement.
claims.limit: Not a citywide rule that every adopted person was enslaved or every breach was actually punished this way.
claims.relevance: A status-changing sanction must remain distinct from a person’s status when the contract was drawn up.
claims.interpretations: The contract creates heirs and threatens a coercive consequence for a specified breach. Those facts should not be collapsed into one status label.

claims.title: Paid manumission with qualified Nippur attribution
claims.claim: BE 6/2 8 records Ištar-rabiat’s manumission, a payment of ten shekels to Duššubtum, and protection against named heirs’ future claims; its Nippur attribution requires a provenance qualification.
claims.context: CBS 9183, P264577; probable Nippur documentary origin, conflicting historical find attribution, no secure house/locus
claims.etype: Primary edition plus current provenance research/catalogue
claims.secondary: AMAS2026 p. 116 nn. 7–8 supports Nippur from internal evidence; CDLI adopted this attribution in 2026.
claims.counter: Poebel labels the tablet Yokha. Neither the source of the payment nor later residence is stated.
claims.rationale: The manumission/payment content is explicit, but inclusion as Nippur evidence depends on an argued attribution rather than a secure archaeological context.
claims.limit: Not securely excavated domestic evidence, not a general slave savings right, and not evidence that manumission always ended other dependence.
claims.relevance: Preserves an attested status change and transaction while separating documentary origin, legal effect, and subsequent livelihood.
claims.interpretations: Use as attributed Nippur evidence, excluded from a strictly findspot-secure subset. The protected heirs named in the clause belong to the former owner’s succession, not an identified family of the freed woman.

claims.title: Institutional livelihood rights in family property
claims.claim: BE 6/2 43 places a six-month annual Enlil priestly office share and associated livelihood land within a family property division.
claims.etype: Primary edition, with catalogue corroboration for transferable office terms
claims.primary: BE 6/2 43, P1909 pp. 22–23; catalogue p. 150. SZ1976 nos. 19 and 32 provide additional office-transfer leads.
claims.secondary: The report uses “office share/right” for the economic relationship without asserting a fully reconstructed service regime.
claims.counter: Possession of rights does not prove that the holder personally performed every duty or establish residence in a temple.
claims.rationale: The temporal share and associated support land are explicit in the published division.
claims.limit: This office arrangement, not an institutional labor taxonomy or an assumption that all temple-linked people were dependents of one type.
claims.relevance: Household property and institution-linked livelihood could intersect without making them interchangeable.
claims.interpretations: The recipient’s claim is legible in a kin/property agreement; the document is not a schedule of daily work or evidence for how substitutes were organized.

claims.title: Cultivation through a lease, not a personal hire
claims.claim: BE 6/2 29 records Damu-idinnam’s lease of Ibgatum’s field for cultivation at one-third of returns as annual rent.
claims.secondary: Poebel distinguishes the field lease from the personal hire of BE 6/2 51.
claims.counter: The labor force, household residence, and lessee’s broader status are not specified.
claims.rationale: The object, purpose, and return-based rent are explicit in the edition.
claims.limit: Not proof of tenant enslavement, self-performed labor, or a standard tenancy arrangement throughout the city.
claims.relevance: An economic obligation to produce or render returns does not by itself identify the legal status of the cultivator.
claims.interpretations: Separate access to land and its returns from a contract for a named person’s labor. Whether the lessee used relatives, hired workers, or enslaved labor is an open question for this case.

claims.title: Marital breach clauses vary
claims.claim: BE 6/2 48 and 40 prescribe different consequences for a wife’s repudiation: the former includes sale, while the latter specifies financial consequences.
claims.period: Samsu-iluna 18/IV/1 and 13/I; day of BE 40 not fixed here
claims.context: Nippur; Naramtum/Awilia and Ama-sukkal/Enlil-idzu; Ni 1919 and CBS 7018
claims.primary: BE 6/2 48 and 40, P1909 pp. 35–38; SZ1976 no. 24 identifies the case of BE 40.
claims.secondary: The physical marking clause in BE 48 has a doubtful rendering in P1909; it is not used here to reconstruct a specific punishment technique.
claims.counter: Neither text records actual repudiation or punishment. BE 40 directly blocks a uniform sale-rule generalization from BE 48.
claims.rationale: The contrast rests on explicit contractual provisions in two documents, not an inferred social ranking.
claims.limit: Two agreements; not a comprehensive account of marriage law, women’s legal position, or enforcement.
claims.relevance: Legal vulnerability can be relationship- and clause-specific rather than a permanent status inferred from gender alone.
claims.interpretations: The difference is historically meaningful without proving why these parties used different terms. Social class, prior circumstances, or legal practice cannot be selected as the cause from these documents alone.

claims.title: Instruction without an apprenticeship contract
claims.claim: Nippur educational tablet CBS 14156 provides evidence for instructional copying; it does not itself document an apprenticeship agreement.
claims.period: Old Babylonian; no regnal date assigned here
claims.context: Nippur educational artifact; no household-membership attribution made
claims.etype: Original study of a primary artifact
claims.primary: CBS 14156, illustrated in T1998 p. 45 fig. 9.
claims.secondary: Tinney identifies teacher-model and student-practice portions.
claims.counter: No fees, duration of service, indenture, kin relation, or residence follows from those features.
claims.rationale: Instruction is supported, but the social and contractual relation is unrecorded.
claims.limit: Not an attested paid apprenticeship or resident pupil.
claims.relevance: Separates skill transmission from legally specified labor service.
claims.interpretations: The educational object answers a narrower question than a service contract would.

claims.title: Model manumissions are not event records
claims.claim: Nippur manumission model contracts must be treated as didactic evidence, not counted as completed releases of named people.
claims.period: Old Babylonian; individual regnal dating not established here
claims.context: Nippur model corpus, especially TMH 11 1 as reported by Spada
claims.etype: Specialist analysis; primary model edition not directly consulted
claims.primary: TMH 11 1, identified through SP2021 p. 287 n. 13; SP2018 not directly read.
claims.secondary: Spada distinguishes the pedagogical corpus from actual legal records.
claims.counter: Her separately edited examples have mixed or uncertain provenances; not all are Nippur.
claims.rationale: The genre distinction is clear, but the underlying Nippur edition was not directly checked.
claims.limit: No event frequency or actual individual life history can be generated from these examples.
claims.relevance: Prevents didactic names and formulae from becoming invented social biographies.
claims.interpretations: Formulae can frame a legal question; their occurrence on a school text is not proof of a corresponding transaction.
